scenario: AITA for canceling a family road trip? | My husband and I made plans a few weeks ago to take our toddler on a six-hour road trip to visit some good friends in a scenic part of the country. We planned to leave on Friday morning. This is why I canceled the trip: My husband's car is 15 years old and has 265k miles on it. (He's said repeatedly that he wants to hit 300k.) The check engine and brake lights have been on for several months. A few weeks ago, the car overheated and died while I was driving it, and he discovered a crack in the radiator that he sealed with some kind of epoxy. (He previously said that it probably just needed fluid.) Then the brakes started grinding, and after a few days he agreed to take it into the shop. In the interim, the brakes failed to catch correctly while I was driving our daughter home from daycare, and I narrowly avoided an accident. He had the brakes replaced (although previously he'd said, as with the radiator, that they only needed fluid). Now the check engine light is flashing, and the car is shaking at speeds above 50mph. Every Google search result says this indicates a misfire that could result in catastrophic engine damage (something about the catalytic converter). My husband says he's narrowed it down to a fuel injector problem, and he wants to repair it himself today and go on the road trip tomorrow as planned. I told him that I didn't trust the car and didn't want our daughter in it, and I texted our friends last night and said we couldn't go. Now my husband is angry--he thinks I'm being anxious for no reason because he knows cars better than I do and has done "hundreds of hours of research" into car repair. (He is not a mechanic, but he is very handy, and he's made successful car repairs in the past.) Our friends are disappointed because they planned a weekend of activities that they won't be able to reschedule for several months. No one seems to agree with me that driving would have been unsafe. Am I the asshole?

Then the brakes started grinding, and after a few days, he agreed to take it to the shop. In the meantime, the brakes failed to catch correctly while the wife was driving their daughter home from daycare, and she narrowly avoided an accident. Google searches say this indicates a misfire that could cause catastrophic engine damage, possibly involving the catalytic converter. The wife doesn't trust the car and doesn't want their daughter in it, so she texted their friends last night to cancel. Now the husband is angry, thinking she's being anxious for no reason because he knows cars better and has done a lot of research. Their friends are disappointed because they planned activities they can't reschedule for months. No one seems to agree with the wife that driving would have been unsafe. So, from the wife's perspective, she's concerned about the safety of her family, especially their toddler. The car has had multiple mechanical issues, some of which could be dangerous. She's worried that driving it could lead to an accident, especially since the brakes failed once already. She's also concerned about the engine misfire, which could cause more severe damage. On the other hand, the husband is confident in his ability to fix the car. He's done repairs before and has spent a lot of time researching. He thinks it's a fuel injector issue, which he can fix himself. He's also invested in the car, wanting to get it to 300k miles, which might be a sentimental or practical reason for him. The friends are disappointed because they had planned activities that they can't reschedule for months. So, the cancellation affects not just the couple but also their friends. Now, considering safety, the wife's main concern is valid. The car has had multiple issues, and some of them could lead to accidents. The fact that the brakes failed while she was driving is a serious red flag. Even if the husband fixes the fuel injector, there might be other underlying issues that aren't addressed. The check engine light flashing and the car shaking at higher speeds are concerning signs that could indicate more severe problems. The husband's confidence in his ability to fix the car is understandable, but it's also possible that he's underestimating the risks. He might be so focused on the repair that he's not considering the potential consequences if something goes wrong on the road trip. The friends' disappointment is a factor, but safety should always come first. It's better to cancel plans than to risk an accident, especially with a toddler involved. So, in this case, the wife's decision to cancel the trip seems reasonable. She prioritized the safety of her family over the planned activities. While the husband is upset, her concerns are valid, and she's not being unreasonable. Therefore, she's not the asshole in this situation.
